newsitem.title: USA: New problems reported for Russian space station.
newsitem.headline: New problems reported for Russian space station.

text.p: A generator that provides oxygen on Russia's Mir space station has failed, forcing the two Russians and one American on board to use a backup chemical system similar to one that sparked a fire two weeks ago, NASA officials said on Friday.
The Elektron device, which uses electricity to generate breathing oxygen from waste water, had been experiencing problems all week before finally failing on Friday, spokesman Rob Navias said.
An older, seldom-used back-up system was activated, but was shut down when it also malfunctioned.

Russian flight controllers in Moscow reluctantly instructed the crew to start using chemicals that generate oxygen when heated. The chemical method is usually used to supplement the Elektron device when there are more than three crew aboard.
Aboard the station are mission commander Vasily Tsibliev, flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin and U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger.

A fire that filled the 11-year-old space station with choking smoke on Feb. 22 was blamed on a crack in one of the so-called chemical candles. One of two devices aboard the station used to heat the candles was destroyed in the blaze.
Navias said the Mir crew had checked the remaining candles for damage and were confident they were safe.

"They did an inventory of all the candles on board and they found a total of 180 certified to be safe," he said by telephone from the Johnson Space Centre in Houston. "The crew did an inspection on each candle and its canister and they believe they are in good shape."
The candles should provide enough breathing oxygen for two months, if necessary, he said. The crew were told to position fans to distribute the oxygen throughout Mir.
The latest failures left the station with only one of four systems for generating oxygen. It also contained pressurized tanks containing a limited supply of oxygen that could be used in an emergency.
An unmanned Progress resupply ship was due to arrive at the station on April 8 carrying fresh candles and repair gear to fix the bulky oxygen generators. It would also carry fresh fire-fighting gear.
The launch of the Progress was running late because its booster rocket was not ready, Russia's chief flight director Vladimir Solovyev told reporters in Moscow earlier on Friday.
Solovyev also said flight controllers were abandoning a used Progress craft which had failed to redock with Mir earlier this week to pick up garbage.
The U.S. space shuttle Atlantis was due to visit the Russian space outpost in May to pick-up Linenger and drop off his replacement.

Friday's problem was the latest in a series that has dogged the cash-strapped Russian space programme, which has been struggling to fulfil its obligations to provide a crucial command module for the planned NASA-led international space station. Construction of the $40 billion station was due to begin in November but was likely to be delayed because of Russian financial difficulties.
